title: Final: sorting, intervals and greedy
sub: Recognize the technique from the statement, predict a merge, spot a wrong sort, test a greedy with a counterexample
cards/0/q: Meeting Rooms (#252): meetings [start, end), n up to 10⁴. Can one person attend all of them? Which technique?
cards/0/options/0: Sort by start and compare neighbours: start[i] < end[i − 1] is a conflict; O(n log n)
cards/0/options/1: Check every pair — you cannot beat O(n²)
cards/0/options/2: Sort by length and check starting from the short ones
cards/0/explain: After sorting by start, only the previous meeting can overlap a meeting — the same thought as "only the last block matters" in Merge Intervals. Meetings are half-open, so the sign is strict: ending at 10 and starting at 10 is not a conflict.
cards/0/wrong/1: Pairs are unnecessary: if meeting i does not overlap the previous one by start, it does not overlap earlier ones either — they ended even sooner, or a conflict has already been found.
cards/0/wrong/2: Length does not determine who overlaps whom. Sorting by start is what makes meetings neighbours in time.
cards/0/wrong/3: Kadane finds the subarray with the largest sum — it does not check overlaps in time.

cards/2/task: A new input: [5, 8] [1, 2] [6, 7] [2, 4] [10, 13] [13, 14] [9, 10]. Step through the trace; the rig sorts the intervals by start and asks once what the code will do.
cards/2/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: The block becomes [1, 8]: 4 and 5 are adjacent integers
cards/2/goal/asks/0/q: The last block is [1, 4]. The next by start is [5, 8]. What does the code do?
cards/2/goal/asks/0/explain: An interval is every point from its start to its end, not a set of integers: between 4 and 5 lies (4, 5), which belongs to no interval. The condition iv[0] <= res[^1][1] — 5 ≤ 4 — is false, so a new block opens. Next, [6, 7] falls inside [5, 8], while [9, 10], [10, 13] and [13, 14] merge by touching: the answer is [1, 4] [5, 8] [9, 14].
cards/3/q: Non-overlapping Intervals: on [[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]] the code returns 2, but the answer is 1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/3/explain: Sorting by start: [1, 100] is taken first, the line moves to 100, and both short ones are removed. The greedy choice in this problem is the earliest end: a[1].CompareTo(b[1]). Then [2, 3] and [4, 5] stay and only [1, 100] is removed. The rest of the code is correct.
cards/4/q: Every frame, 2000 transparent particles of your own system must be sorted back to front; there are no layers, depth ≥ 0. What is cheapest?
cards/4/options/0: The key is ~(depth bits) as a uint, then Array.Sort(keys, ids, 0, count)
cards/4/options/2: List.Sort with a lambda that computes the distance to the camera in every comparison
cards/4/options/3: Two List.Sort calls: first by id, then by depth
cards/4/explain: For a float ≥ 0 the bits grow with the value, and inverting them gives "far ones first". The keys are uints: direct comparison without a delegate, only the filled part is sorted, no new objects.
cards/4/wrong/1: OrderByDescending creates a buffer, key and index arrays and a result array every frame — garbage for the GC.
cards/4/wrong/2: The distance is computed about 2·n·log₂ n times instead of n, plus a delegate call per comparison, and capturing the camera creates a closure.
cards/4/wrong/3: The second Sort will not keep the id order — it is unstable. Nor is it needed: equal depths decide nothing for transparents.
cards/5/q: Coins 1, 6, 10, sum 12. What does greedy change-making ("the largest coin that fits") give, and what is the optimum?
cards/5/options/0: Greedy gives 3 coins (10 + 1 + 1), the optimum is 2 (6 + 6) — you need DP
cards/5/options/1: Greedy gives 2 coins — that is the optimum
cards/5/options/2: Greedy gives 3 coins — and that is the optimum
cards/5/options/3: Greedy finds no change at all
cards/5/explain: Greedy takes 10, and the remaining 2 can only be ones: three coins. But 6 + 6 is two. As with 1, 3, 4: no optimal solution starts with the largest coin, the exchange fails, so you need DP over sums.
cards/5/wrong/1: After the ten, 2 is left, and a six does not fit into 2: only 1 + 1.
cards/5/wrong/2: 6 + 6 = 12 is two coins, fewer than three.
cards/5/wrong/3: There is a one, so greedy always covers the remainder — the only question is how many coins.
cards/6/q: Prices [3, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6], unlimited deals (holding at most one share). What is the largest profit?
cards/6/explain: The sum of all rises: 5 − 3 = 2, 4 − 1 = 3, 6 − 2 = 4 — 9 in total. Each rise is a separate deal, and the falls are skipped.
cards/6/wrong/1: 5 is a single deal (buy at 1, sell at 6), problem #121. Here deals are unlimited.
cards/6/wrong/2: That is two deals out of three: 3 + 4. The rise 3 → 5 is profitable too.
cards/6/wrong/3: That is only the rise 1 → 4. There are also 3 → 5 and 2 → 6.
cards/7/q: A new problem: Meeting Rooms II (#253) — how many rooms meetings [start, end) need. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: are meetings half-open? Do an end at 10 and a start at 10 share one room?
cards/7/items/1: Naive: for each start, count the meetings in progress at that moment — O(n²)
cards/7/items/2: The idea: a sweep — a start is +1, an end is −1, the answer is the peak of the sum
cards/7/items/3: Code: starts and ends in two sorted arrays, two pointers, ends before starts
cards/7/items/5: Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the array copies
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: no meetings, all at once, back-to-back meetings
cards/7/explain: The answer to the back-to-back question decides the sign in the code: e[j] <= s[i], ends before starts. The example [0, 30) [5, 10) [15, 20) shows that the second and third meetings can share the same room.
cards/8/q: What is true about complexity? Select all that apply.
cards/8/options/0: Merge Intervals is O(n log n), because of the sort
cards/8/options/1: Insert Interval on sorted input is O(n)
cards/8/options/2: Array.Sort is O(n²) in the worst case
cards/8/options/3: Counting sort of 10⁶ values from 0 to 100 is O(n + k)
cards/8/options/4: Two-pass Candy is O(n) time and O(1) memory
cards/8/options/5: Kadane is O(n) time and O(1) memory
cards/8/explain: Merging is a sort plus a pass. Insertion needs no sort: three phases in one pass. Counting is n for the counters and k for the prefixes. Kadane keeps two numbers. But Array.Sort is introspective: on deep recursion it switches to heapsort, so the worst case is O(n log n). Two-pass Candy stores the candy array — O(n) memory.
